questions.title: How does the DPO loss (Eq. 9) avoid the need for a learned baseline or reward normalization?
questions.question_body: In the standard RLHF pipeline, after fitting a reward model we usually need to subtract a baseline (e.g., the mean reward or a value function) when computing the policy gradient to reduce variance. The DPO paper claims that by re‑parameterising the reward as \(\hat r_\theta(x,y)=\beta\log\frac{\pi_\theta(y|x)}{\pi_{ref}(y|x)}\) the loss in Eq. 9 does not require any baseline term. Could someone explain intuitively why the partition function \(Z(x)\) cancels out and why this eliminates the need for an explicit baseline? How does this relate to the weighting term \(\sigma(\hat r_\theta(x,y_l)-\hat r_\theta(x,y_w))\) in the gradient (Eq. 10)?

questions.title: Why does the optimal policy for the KL‑constrained RL objective have the form in Eq. 5?
questions.question_body: Equation 5 states that the optimal policy under the objective \( \max_{\pi}\, \mathbb{E}[r(x,y)] - \beta \mathrm{KL}(\pi||\pi_{ref}) \) is \( \pi_r(y|x)=\frac{1}{Z(x)}\pi_{ref}(y|x)\exp\bigl(\frac{1}{\beta}r(x,y)\bigr) \). I understand this looks like a Boltzmann distribution, but I’m not sure how the KL‑constraint leads to this exact closed‑form solution. Could anyone provide a short derivation (e.g., using Lagrange multipliers) or point to a reference that shows why this is true?

questions.title: What role does the reference model \(\pi_{ref}\) play when it is initialized from an SFT model vs. when it is learned from preferred completions only?
questions.question_body: The DPO algorithm requires a reference policy \(\pi_{ref}\). The paper mentions two ways of obtaining it: (1) using the SFT model if it is available, and (2) learning it by maximizing likelihood of preferred completions when no SFT model exists. How does this choice affect the term \(\log \frac{\pi_\theta(y|x)}{\pi_{ref}(y|x)}\) in the loss? In particular, does learning \(\pi_{ref}\) from only preferred data bias the KL‑constraint, and could that explain any performance differences observed in the dialogue experiments?

questions.title: How does DPO handle multiple comparisons per prompt (e.g., Plackett‑Luce rankings) instead of binary preferences?
questions.question_body: The derivation in Section 4 mainly discusses binary preferences modeled by Bradley‑Terry. The appendix mentions extensions to Plackett‑Luce models for rankings of more than two answers. Could someone clarify how Eq. 9 would change for a dataset where each prompt has a ranked list of three or more completions? What would be the appropriate loss function and does the same "reward = β log π/π_ref" reparameterisation still hold?

questions.title: Why does naïve unlikelihood training (without DPO’s weighting) cause model degeneration?
questions.question_body: The paper states that a naïve version of DPO that simply maximises \(\log \pi_θ(y_w|x) - \log \pi_θ(y_l|x)\) (i.e., unlikelihood on dispreferred outputs) leads to degeneration, whereas DPO’s weighted gradient prevents this. What is the precise mechanism behind this degeneration? Is it related to pushing down probabilities of dispreferred tokens too aggressively, causing mode collapse, or something else? Any empirical evidence or toy example would help.

questions.title: What equivalence class of reward functions is represented by the DPO reparameterisation?
questions.question_body: Theorem 1 claims that any reward function consistent with Bradley‑Terry can be written as \(r(x,y)=\beta \log \frac{π(y|x)}{π_{ref}(y|x)}+c(x)\). I understand Lemma 1 and Lemma 2 about preference and policy invariance within an equivalence class, but I’m confused about what freedom remains after fixing \(π(y|x)\). Does DPO implicitly fix the additive term \(c(x)\) to zero, and if so, how does this affect identifiability? Could there be useful reward functions that cannot be captured because they require a non‑constant \(c(x)\)?

questions.title: How is the KL‑target hyperparameter (β) chosen in practice and how does it affect the reward–KL trade‑off?
questions.question_body: In experiments β values such as 0.05, 0.1, 1, 5 are tried. Smaller β seems to enforce stronger KL regularisation while larger β allows more reward optimisation. Is there a principled way to set β (e.g., based on desired KL budget or on properties of the reference model), or is it purely empirical? Also, how does β interact with temperature at generation time?

questions.title: Can DPO be combined with self‑training / preference bootstrapping on unlabeled prompts?
questions.question_body_hist: The discussion mentions future work on self‑labeling from the DPO policy. Since DPO directly yields an implicit reward via \(π/π_{ref}\), is there a straightforward way to generate synthetic preferences for new prompts by comparing two samples from π_θ and then add them to D? Would that preserve convergence guarantees, or could it amplify bias?
